lesson.title: Balancing the Books: Conserving Atoms in a Chemical Equation
lesson.summary: Balancing a chemical equation means adjusting coefficients, never subscripts, until the same number of each type of atom appears on both sides, honoring the law of conservation of mass.
lesson.body:
The whole practice of balancing rests on a single physical fact from Conservation Laws: in an ordinary chemical reaction, atoms are neither created nor destroyed, only rearranged into new combinations. If a Chemical Equation is going to be a faithful record of that rearrangement, it has to show exactly the same number of each type of atom on the reactant side as on the product side. An equation that fails this test, like the unbalanced H2 + O2 -> H2O from the previous chapter, is not just untidy, it is claiming that an oxygen atom appeared from nowhere, which cannot happen.

The one and only tool available for fixing this is the coefficient: the whole number placed in front of a formula that says how many units of that substance are involved. Coefficients can be changed freely, including being left as an implied 1 when nothing is written. What can never be changed is a subscript inside a formula, because a subscript is part of what defines the compound itself; changing H2O to H2O2 does not balance an equation, it silently swaps water for hydrogen peroxide, an entirely different substance with entirely different chemistry. This distinction, adjusting coefficients but never subscripts, is the single most important rule in this chapter.

A reliable strategy is to balance elements that appear in only one reactant and one product first, and save elements that appear alone, uncombined, for last, since a lone element is the easiest thing to adjust once everything else is fixed. Let's apply that strategy to the rusting of iron: Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3. Iron appears once on each side, but oxygen is the more constrained element here because O2 always comes in pairs while Fe2O3 needs oxygen in groups of three, so start with oxygen. The left side supplies oxygen two atoms at a time (from O2), while the right side needs oxygen three atoms at a time (from Fe2O3). The smallest number divisible by both 2 and 3 is 6, so aim for six oxygen atoms on each side: put a 3 in front of O2, giving 3 times 2 = 6 oxygen atoms, and put a 2 in front of Fe2O3, giving 2 times 3 = 6 oxygen atoms. The equation now reads Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3. With oxygen settled, check iron: the right side now has 2 Fe2O3, contributing 2 times 2 = 4 iron atoms, so the left side needs a coefficient of 4 in front of Fe. The finished, balanced equation is 4 Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3.

Verify it atom by atom, the way you should always check your own work. Left side: 4 Fe gives 4 iron atoms, and 3 O2 gives 3 times 2 = 6 oxygen atoms, for a total of 4 Fe and 6 O. Right side: 2 Fe2O3 gives 2 times 2 = 4 iron atoms and 2 times 3 = 6 oxygen atoms, again 4 Fe and 6 O. Both sides match, so the equation is balanced and honors conservation of mass exactly as required.

A few pitfalls are worth flagging. If a coefficient makes another atom count come out as a fraction partway through your work, do not leave a fractional coefficient in a final answer; instead, multiply every coefficient in the entire equation by whatever whole number clears the fraction. And when a formula contains a polyatomic group like NO3 or SO4 that survives unchanged from one side to the other, it is often faster to balance that entire group as a single unit rather than counting its individual atoms separately. Both tricks save time once basic balancing, like the iron oxide example above, feels automatic.
